Despite the Northern Territory government’s multimillion-dollar pledge to bolster a cuts-ravaged Legal Aid NT, the majority of the additional funding has been withheld.

Seven months after Legal Aid NT drastically cut its assistance to people charged with criminal offences, a budget estimates committee has heard that most of a promised multimillion-dollar funding increase from the Northern Territory government has not been provided.

With its landslide win in August 2024, the Country Liberal Party (CLP) inherited from Territory Labor an indebted and chronically underfunded legal aid agency. By mid 2025, NT attorney-general Marie-Clare Boothby had appointed not just a new Legal Aid NT director, Catherine Voumard, but also an entirely new board of commissioners, and substantially increased its funding.

“We need Legal Aid because we need justice for victims,” Boothby declared in May last year. “We have given Legal Aid certainty of funding, an extra $5.5 million ongoing, year after year.” Legal Aid NT reported an operating surplus for 2024/25 of nearly $2 million.

Nobody anticipated the cuts that were to come just six months later. On November 17, Voumard wrote to lawyers advising of the cuts, which were effective immediately, and cited only a projected “end of financial year deficit”. Legal aid was no longer available to anyone on bail. She supplied no data and no further explanation and has not responded to queries from journalists – including The Saturday Paper, which has put questions to Voumard and Legal Aid NT on multiple occasions.

Meanwhile, Boothby continued to insist she had fixed Legal Aid NT’s longstanding problems. “Rubbish and nonsense” was how she described allegations that the CLP had cut the agency’s budget. “It was our government, just after coming to government, that increased Legal Aid funding by 87 per cent,” she told parliament in March this year.

At that time, there was no way of assessing her claim. Neither Legal Aid NT’s annual reports nor the government’s budget papers report the dollar amounts the Territory government grants to its legal aid agency each year. Boothby did not say that most of the extra funds announced had been withheld.

It was only when the Criminal Lawyers Association of the Northern Territory (CLANT) sent Voumard a letter in April seeking an explanation that she broke her silence. The Legal Aid head explained that the CLP had cut her agency’s 2025/26 funding by 21 per cent compared with 2024/25. Boothby’s 87 per cent increase applied only to “baseline” funding and did not include reimbursements and top-ups the agency had usually received. The higher baseline funding was not sufficient, Voumard wrote, given the “growth in overall demand” for the agency’s services, and the increased costs of providing those services. She gave no further details, nor did she disclose that funds had been withheld.

Boothby later countered that the higher 2024/25 funding was a one-off injection to help the agency cope with a temporary rise in referrals from the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency (NAAJA), and that situation had since resolved. The attorney-general began circulating data showing the 2025/26 funding was 19 per cent higher than the total amount it had received – including in reimbursements and top-ups – in 2023/24.

In a letter to the federal attorney-general, Michelle Rowland, on May 22, Boothby made no mention of having withheld the allocated funds.

“I offered Legal Aid, at its request, a multi-year funding agreement, which it had asked for over a long time,” she told parliament in May. “That conversation started in May last year; a year later that is still unsigned by Legal Aid.”

She then offered something new: “It is Legal Aid not wanting to do the work and make the changes for its own organisation and to sign a multi-year funding agreement so that we can give the money over. Okay?”

Asked to clarify whether Legal Aid NT had received any of the additional $5.5 million allocated to it, Boothby referred this paper back to Legal Aid NT and Voumard, who did not respond.

In response to the same question, a spokesperson for the Attorney-General’s Department told The Saturday Paper on June 12: “Of the $12.799 million in NT Government funding available to Legal Aid NT, $8.396 million has been released to date, with the remainder” – $4.403 million – “subject to the execution of a funding agreement”.

It was the first time anyone across the NT government had confirmed that most of the additional funding had not been provided to Legal Aid NT. The Saturday Paper supplied the department’s response to the independent member for Johnston, Justine Davis, to inform her questions in this week’s budget estimates hearing. The Saturday Paper also forwarded the department’s response to the NT attorney-general, whose adviser again simply deferred to Legal Aid NT, and to Voumard, who did not respond.

“I can’t understand [Voumard’s] strategy. She’s clearly pissed off the government. But she’s also not bringing the legal profession in so that we can help her to advocate for whatever she needs. And she’s just not saying anything.”

On Wednesday in estimates, Boothby confirmed – publicly for the first time, in response to questions from Davis and Labor’s shadow attorney-general, Chansey Paech – that $4.403 million of the additional $5.5 million earmarked for Legal Aid NT had been withheld because the agency had not signed the funding agreement it had been offered in May 2025.

Davis asked Boothby to explain the sticking point in negotiations. “I cannot go into the detail of that,” Boothby replied. “The department had many conversations with Legal Aid over the last 12 months. They still have not signed that multi-year agreement. I do not know why. That is a question for Legal Aid.”

Voumard did not appear at the estimates hearing on Wednesday.

“The expectation is that they sign that agreement,” the NT attorney-general said. “Part of that agreement is when the department asks for information from Legal Aid, that the information is forthcoming. That has been a real challenge ...

“The department has asked what exactly is required for a full return of service to deliver,” Boothby told estimates, “and we have not heard back from Legal Aid about what is required.”

In Voumard’s absence, Paech and Davis asked Boothby to confirm the number of services Legal Aid NT has provided this year, so that Voumard’s claims – of greater demand and higher costs – can be evaluated. “It is a great question,” the attorney-general said. She said her department had asked Legal Aid NT to provide this information, and the agency had not done so. She took the question on notice.

One major source of demand for Legal Aid NT’s criminal defence services has been the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency, whose referrals accounted for about half of Legal Aid NT’s workload until 2022/23. No data has been published since then, and The Saturday Paper has asked both Legal Aid NT and NAAJA for recent figures. A spokesperson said the Aboriginal justice agency is “not in a position to provide data on referrals at this stage”. Legal Aid NT did not respond.

On Wednesday, Paech asked the NT attorney-general to supply data confirming the numbers of NAAJA referrals to Legal Aid NT. “When we have asked NAAJA and Legal Aid for that data, the numbers do not match up,” Boothby said. “There are some anomalies there, so we have gone back to them and asked them for more data.”

The Saturday Paper understands that CLANT has again written to Voumard recently, asking her to explain to the legal profession why Legal Aid NT has not signed the agreement for over a year, and why she has preferred to cut services. The lawyers association declined to comment to this paper before it receives Voumard’s reply.

The Saturday Paper also understands that Legal Aid NT staff were told in a meeting this week to be sceptical of what appears in media reports, and that Legal Aid NT is attempting to negotiate with the government. However, staff have confirmed to this paper that they had also not been told the additional funding had been withheld, nor that the agency had not signed the agreement.

“I can’t understand [Voumard’s] strategy,” says one criminal lawyer who accepts briefs from Legal Aid NT. “She’s clearly pissed off the government. But she’s also not bringing the legal profession in so that we can help her to advocate for whatever she needs. And she’s just not saying anything.”

Questions remain as to why Boothby appointed Voumard director of Legal Aid NT in May 2025, despite Voumard’s lack of managerial experience or qualifications. She had been employed by the now deputy chief minister, Gerard Maley, in 2014, when he was running the law firm of his brother during Peter Maley’s brief and controversial tenure as a magistrate. She has also since worked for NAAJA, Legal Aid and as a prosecutor. In two rounds of recruitment for the Legal Aid role, Voumard was not an endorsed candidate.

Voumard’s appointment to lead Legal Aid NT reportedly prompted the resignations of at least three board commissioners and an unknown number of staff.

“She was extremely unwise to accept that appointment, in my view,” one Darwin barrister tells The Saturday Paper. “The director’s gig was always going to be difficult under this government, even for an experienced administrator. Frankly, Catherine [Voumard] was a lamb to the slaughter.”

Despite Boothby’s efforts to shift the blame for the service cuts to Voumard, the attorney-general remains ultimately responsible for the agency’s failures. The Saturday Paper asked Boothby whether she continues to have confidence in Voumard and the board of commissioners she appointed. “Legal Aid NT is an independent statutory body and questions about their operations, management and media engagement are matters for them,” Boothby said.

The Saturday Paper again sought comment from Voumard following Boothby’s estimates appearance on Wednesday. Again, Voumard did not respond by deadline.

The ongoing service cuts mean that even defendants in custody are not afforded legal aid after the agency has spent a monthly cap. The limit for this month was reached on June 5.

Earlier this month, the Northern Territory Supreme Court confirmed that courts are obliged to “stay”, or pause, the prosecution of defendants who are unrepresented because legal aid is unavailable to them and they can’t afford a lawyer. On Wednesday in Katherine, and on the previous Friday in Darwin, dozens of self-represented defendants appeared in special lists so the Local Court could begin to manage their requests for stays.

“I need to put on the record that I do not accept that those alleged offenders are without representation,” Boothby told estimates. Yet a minute later she confirmed she was aware that “about 20” stay applications had already been made.

Presumably more will follow. But the attorney-general also said she’d instructed her department to come up with a plan to ensure that those defendants will be represented, even if Legal Aid NT doesn’t do it.

The author works for a law firm that accepts referrals from Legal Aid NT and NAAJA. Any views expressed in this article are his own.

Russell Marks is an adjunct research fellow at La Trobe University and works as a criminal defence lawyer in the Northern Territory.
